title: What the truck: Hauling antimatter at CERN
excerpt: After a successful first road trip, antimatter could one day be delivered by vehicle to university labs.
content:
After a successful first road trip, antimatter could one day be delivered by vehicle to university labs.

“All he needed was a wheel in his hand and four on the road,” writes Jack Kerouac in his 1957 novel, On the Road. If he’d been at CERN this year, he might’ve have added one more element: a refrigerator-sized box holding nearly 100 antiprotons.

CERN scientists drove the trapped antiprotons from CERN’s Antimatter Factory around the campus earlier this year. The antiprotons were stored in a battery-powered and liquid-hydrogen-cooled electromagnetic trap—called a Penning trap—during transit. The researchers have now published an article about the journey in Nature.

Charged antiparticles, like antiprotons, have the same mass as their particle counterparts but the opposite charge. Antimatter, which consists of antiparticles, is created naturally through various processes, such as when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and is produced artificially for research purposes in particle-physics laboratories, like the ones at the Antimatter Factory.

“For trapped antiprotons, it was the first time that they left the building, so it’s a historic moment,” says Christian Smorra, a scientist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany and a member of CERN’s BASE (Baryon Antibaryon Symmetry Experiment) collaboration. Smorra spoke with Physics Today about taking antimatter for a spin as part of the BASE-STEP (Symmetry Tests in Experiments with Portable Antiprotons) project and what inspired the road trip in the first place.

The following interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Why is antimatter so hard to transport?

If antiprotons come into contact with any kind of other particle, it annihilates. One hard thing about transporting antimatter is that you need an ultrahigh-vacuum chamber in the Penning trap. The background pressure of the vacuum defines the collision rate between the trapped antiprotons and the residual gas.

A standard vacuum chamber with 10−9 millibar pressure gives you a lifetime of about a second for an antiproton before it collides with a residual particle and annihilates. What we needed for the transport antiproton trap is a vacuum with 10−16 millibar pressure, seven orders of magnitude smaller than a standard vacuum, to get an antiproton lifetime of several months.

Why transport antimatter?

I work on the BASE project at CERN’s Antiproton Decelerator facility in Geneva that makes high-precision measurements of the magnetic moment of antiprotons.

Eight years ago, Stefan Ulmer and I started to discuss that we would need to relocate the precision measurements. We would have much better measurement conditions if we had a laboratory without the magnetic field noise from CERN’s decelerator. A dedicated building like my university lab at the Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf typically has good temperature stability and vibration damping and keeps all the nuisance away. Measuring the antiproton charge-to-mass ratio and the antiproton magnetic moment in a high-precision lab could outperform the measurements in the Antimatter Factory by a factor 10 or 100.

By delivering antiprotons to university labs, we have the possibility to increase the number of antiproton experiments. That’s why I started to look into making the transportable antiproton trap.

How did you transport it?

We built a Penning trap that runs in transport mode that fits through a regular door. The trap uses a superconducting magnet to provide the field to confine the particles, so that needs to be kept cold, and cooling comes from a liquid-helium tank. The system also had a UPS [uninterruptible power supply] battery system. In total, we used 1.6 tons of material to relocate the complete trap.

We put it on a regular 7.5-ton truck and drove it around the CERN campus for about 7 kilometers. You can drive up to 50 kilometers per hour, and there is regular traffic, which helps us see how this system works under normal road conditions.

Christian Smorra explains the antimatter trap used in CERN’s BASE-STEP project. (Video by Piotr Traczyk, with animations by Ivan Snozzi and Maximilien Brice, © 2026 CERN.)

Where were you during the transport? Did you ride along?

I was sitting next to the driver’s seat, and it was probably the most exciting ride of my life.

Is there any way to know during transport if it’s working?

Yes, you can watch live what is happening to the particles in the trap using an electrical oscillator-detection system. That’s good to see, but it’s also stressful. We have done two transports, one with protons two years ago and now one with antiprotons this year. On each trip, the hardware in the detector moved slightly, and for a few seconds, you see the signal showing that the trap is empty. It increases your heart rate if you’re sitting there watching this. But we retuned the detector and saw that we hadn’t lost any particles.

Why study antimatter?

Precision-frontier experiments like BASE could have a big impact on the matter–antimatter symmetry puzzle. Our standard model of particle physics is symmetric in particles and antiparticles, but we observe a matter-filled universe today, and we don’t understand the process that developed the matter excess. If we were to find a trace of an asymmetry between them, then it would completely change the assumptions in cosmology of the early universe.

What got you into this line of research?

I was in an undergraduate physics course in 2006, and there was a lecture about Penning traps and how to measure masses very precisely. That somehow caught my attention, because it’s conceptually very simple to grasp the principle, which is essentially measuring the cyclotron frequency of a charged particle in the magnetic field. But the application has a lot of complexity behind it. I didn’t expect to still be working on the topic 20 years later.

What’s next?

One next step is getting the antiprotons from the transport trap into a laboratory trap system for experiments. We will be working on this for the next two years.

Another step is to make transportation easier and make a miniaturized transportable trap. We are looking at permanent magnet traps systems, because the biggest, and most expensive, part of the transportable trap is the superconducting magnet. We want to downscale it by a factor of two or so in mass and volume. Maybe after this project, we can downscale it even further by another factor of two, and then it should be fairly easy to put it into the back of a van, for example, and then just drive off.
